The order immediately stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets and preserves the status quo pending a hearing on Papaya's petition for formal recognition under Chapter 15.
items.body_md:
On August 9, Judge Mary F. Walrath of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware granted Papaya Gaming's motion for a temporary injunction. 
The order immediately stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets and preserves the status quo pending a hearing on Papaya's petition for formal recognition under Chapter 15.
 
The relief was granted over strong opposition from Firy Inc. (formerly Skillz), whose demands Judge Walrath rejected.
 The injunction is the central near-term protection Papaya sought when it filed: without it, Firy could have moved to attach U.S. assets before recognition is adjudicated, potentially disrupting the Israeli-supervised fund structure on which any eventual recovery to claimants depends.


Judge Cote's underlying July 27 order required Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement plus approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and costs.
 The temporary injunction does not disturb that judgment or Papaya's pending appeal of it; it only freezes enforcement in the U.S. pending the Chapter 15 recognition hearing. For Firy as the sole material creditor, the practical consequence is that U.S.-side collection — including any post-judgment asset discovery or attachment — is halted for now. 
Under the terms Papaya presented to the Israeli court, it will transfer available cash into a designated fund overseen by a court-appointed official, with the fund expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 and additional tens of millions annually, constituting the potential source for claim settlement if the U.S. ruling becomes enforceable in Israel.
 The gap between that fund and the $729 million total exposure remains the defining recovery variable; the recognition hearing will be the next moment at which that gap is formally tested.

Dkts. 56 through 60 — pro hac vice orders for Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo of Latham & Watkins (on Skillz/Firy's behalf) and three further pro hac vice motions filed August 10 — confirm that Firy is assembling a full Latham team alongside its existing Weil Gotshal roster. That concentration of outside counsel on Firy's side signals active preparation for the recognition hearing, consistent with the deposition notices Skillz filed August 8 targeting Oriel Bachar, Pinni Yaniv, and James Kong (Dkts. 53–55). The next concrete milestone is the recognition hearing before Judge Walrath, at which she will determine whether to grant Chapter 15 recognition to the Israeli proceeding and whether the temporary injunction should be extended, modified, or dissolved — no date for that hearing is reflected on the docket as of this briefing.

items.lede: On August 7–8, Skillz filed pro hac vice motions for Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo of Latham & Watkins (Dkts. 50–51), bringing Skillz's admitted Latham team in this proceeding to five attorneys following the Goldberg, Harris, and Schrock admissions entered August 6.
items.body_md:
On August 7–8, Skillz filed pro hac vice motions for Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo of Latham & Watkins (Dkts. 50–51), bringing Skillz's admitted Latham team in this proceeding to five attorneys following the Goldberg, Harris, and Schrock admissions entered August 6. Dkt. 52 is a notice of service. All are procedural and carry no independent weight on recovery or timing.

The substantive posture is unchanged from Saturday's edition. Judge Walrath's temporary injunction — staying collection and enforcement against Papaya's U.S. assets over Skillz's objection — remains the operative protection, as reported by __[Calcalist / CTech](https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/idop8ipjs)__. The Latham buildout does, however, add color to the deposition notices (Dkts. 53–55) filed the same day: Skillz is assembling a full litigation team ahead of the September 3 recognition hearing, not merely preserving rights. The three noticed witnesses — Oriel Bachar, Pinni Yaniv, and James Kong — map directly to the center-of-main-interests question. Yaniv, identified by __[The Jerusalem Post](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-904473)__ as a Meitar Law Offices partner representing Papaya in the Israeli proceeding, is the architect of the Tel Aviv arrangement; his deposition, alongside Bachar's, signals Skillz intends to contest where Papaya actually manages its affairs, not merely argue the legal standard. The financial gap driving that contest has not changed: Judge Cote's disgorgement award stands at approximately $719 million plus approximately $10.1 million in fees and costs per __[Calcalist / CTech](https://www.calcalistech.com/ctechnews/article/idop8ipjs)__, against a supervised Israeli fund expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 per __[World Casino Directory](https://news.worldcasinodirectory.com/papaya-gaming-files-chapter-15-after-719m-verdict-123873)__.

The next hard milestones are the objection deadline of August 27 and the recognition hearing before Judge Walrath on September 3, 2026, at 9:30 AM (virtual). Whether deposition dates for Bachar, Yaniv, and Kong are scheduled and confirmed before August 27 will indicate whether Skillz is building a factual record for a contested COMI challenge at the hearing or using the notices as pre-hearing leverage.

items.lede: The principal development since Friday's briefing is substantive: Judge Walrath's temporary injunction now provides Papaya with legal protection in the United States while the Chapter 15 proceedings move forward. Judge Walrath rejected Skillz's demands and granted Papaya's request.
items.body_md:
The principal development since Friday's briefing is substantive: 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction now provides Papaya with legal protection in the United States while the Chapter 15 proceedings move forward.
 
Judge Walrath rejected Skillz's demands and granted Papaya's request.
 The injunction stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets pending the recognition hearing, which Dkt. 40/41 has already scheduled for September 3, 2026. This is meaningful movement: what the § 1519 provisional stay had established provisionally is now reinforced by a formal injunctive order entered before recognition — a stronger posture for Papaya during the appeal window, and a corresponding constraint on Firy/Skillz's near-term enforcement options in the United States.

That posture is now being tested in discovery. Dkts. 52–55, all filed August 8 by Skillz counsel Sean Beach, are three deposition notices — targeting Oriel Bachar (Papaya's co-founder and CEO), Pinni Yaniv, and James Kong — accompanied by a notice of service. 
Papaya is represented in the Israeli proceeding by attorney Pini Yaniv, a partner in the litigation department at Meitar Law Offices.
 Skillz is plainly using the pre-recognition window to build a factual record, most likely to contest whether the Israeli proceeding qualifies as a foreign main proceeding under 11 U.S.C. § 1517, to challenge the adequacy of the supervised payment arrangement as protection for creditors, or both. The three witnesses span the petitioner herself, Israeli legal counsel, and a third individual whose role is not confirmed in available materials. Dkts. 50 and 51 — pro hac vice motions for Latham & Watkins' Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo, filed August 7 — have now expanded Skillz's Delaware counsel roster to five Latham practitioners, alongside local counsel Beach. That depth of Latham coverage, paired with aggressive pre-hearing discovery, signals that Skillz intends to contest recognition on the merits rather than simply register objections.

From a recovery standpoint, the temporary injunction forecloses the immediate collection path Skillz would need to reach U.S. assets before September 3. The structural ceiling, however, is unchanged: 
Papaya applied to the Tel Aviv District Court for a temporary stay of proceedings, and under the proposed arrangement, the company's available cash and current profits would be transferred to a designated fund held by an authorized representative on behalf of the court — an arrangement intended to safeguard creditors' rights if Papaya's appeal is ultimately rejected.
 That fund was estimated at approximately $100 million during 2026, against a judgment face value of 
approximately $719 million in disgorgement, as well as approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and legal costs.
 The deposition schedule adds procedural complexity before the recognition hearing but does not, by itself, alter that gap. Objections to recognition are due August 27, 2026; the recognition hearing is set for September 3, 2026 at 9:30 AM (virtual).

items.lede: The 72-hour window produced no substantive docket movement. Dkts.
items.body_md:
The 72-hour window produced no substantive docket movement. Dkts. 50 and 51, both filed August 7, are pro hac vice admission motions, continuing the run of practitioner-entry filings that began August 6 (Dkts. 43–49). That brings the two-day total to nine entries — one appearance notice, five pro hac vice motions, and three corresponding admission orders — all procedural, none dispositive. The recognition hearing date set by Dkt. 40 remains the operative next milestone; the date itself is not confirmed in the docket ground truth available and should be verified against PACER directly. The volume of new appearances continues to expand the counsel roster well beyond the debtor and primary judgment creditor, consistent with additional interested parties establishing standing before recognition is decided, but the identities of the newly admitted practitioners are not confirmed in available materials.

One parallel development in the New York proceeding warrants attention as background context. 
The Southern District of New York has a separate opinion addressing Firy's request for injunctive relief that remains forthcoming
 — this was flagged in Firy's July 28 press release but has not yet issued. If Judge Cote enters a broad injunction against Papaya's business practices before the Delaware recognition hearing resolves, the interaction between that order and the § 1519 provisional stay will become a live question: injunctive relief directed at conduct rather than collection would not be automatically stayed by § 1519 or § 1520 in the same way a money judgment enforcement action would be, and Papaya would likely need to seek additional relief or argue the scope of the stay covers it. That is a contingent scenario, not a current one, but the pendency of the injunction opinion means it could materialize on short notice.

The structural recovery constraint remains unchanged: the § 1519 provisional stay is operative, the recognition hearing has been scheduled but not yet heard, and the Israeli-court-supervised fund — expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 — represents the practical ceiling on near-term recovery regardless of what happens in Delaware. The gap between that figure and the $719 million judgment face value (plus approximately $10 million in awarded attorney's fees, per __[Firy Inc. / BusinessWire press release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260728653231/en/Federal-Court-Orders-Papaya-Gaming-to-Pay-$719-Million-to-Skillz-Platform-Inc.-a-FIRY-NYSE-FIRY-Company-Disgorging-Its-Unjust-Profits-From-False-Advertising)__) is not closed by anything that moved this week. The next concrete milestone remains the recognition hearing set by Dkt. 40.

items.lede: The two most consequential filings of the week both landed on August 5. Judge Mary F. Walrath signed Dkt. 39, the Order Granting Provisional Relief Pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 1519 — putting a U.S. statutory stay in place pending the recognition hearing — and simultaneously entered Dkt. 40, the Order Scheduling the Hearing on Recognition of the Chapter 15 Petition and specifying the form and manner of notice.
items.body_md:
The two most consequential filings of the week both landed on August 5. Judge Mary F. Walrath signed Dkt. 39, the Order Granting Provisional Relief Pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 1519 — putting a U.S. statutory stay in place pending the recognition hearing — and simultaneously entered Dkt. 40, the Order Scheduling the Hearing on Recognition of the Chapter 15 Petition and specifying the form and manner of notice. Those two orders together convert what was, through Tuesday, a petition supported only by the Tel Aviv District Court's August 2 domestic stay into a proceeding with active U.S. federal protection. 
If the Delaware court grants full recognition, Firy Inc. (formerly Skillz) would be blocked from collecting on the $719 million judgment while Papaya's appeal runs its course.
 The § 1519 provisional order holds that position in the interim. Dkt. 41, filed the same day, is the notice of hearing distributed to parties; Dkt. 42, filed August 5, is the certificate of service confirming that distribution went out.

Yesterday, August 6, the docket absorbed six more practitioner-entry filings — Dkts. 43 through 49 — consisting of one appearance notice and three pro hac vice motions (Dkts. 44–46) paired with three corresponding admission orders (Dkts. 47–49). Four pro hac vice admissions were already entered by order on August 4 (covering Coleman, Raynal, Carpenito, and Davidson per Dkts. 29–32), so the roster of admitted counsel is now materially larger. That volume of new appearances at this early stage suggests parties beyond the debtor and the primary judgment creditor are positioning themselves in the proceeding — the identities of the newly appearing counsel are not confirmed in the materials available, but the pattern is consistent with additional creditors or interested parties establishing standing ahead of the recognition hearing. The recognition hearing date itself was set by Dkt. 40 but is not confirmed in the current docket ground truth; 
the next key threshold question is whether the U.S. Bankruptcy Court will grant Chapter 15 recognition.


For Firy's recovery posture, the operative tension remains unchanged in structure but has now sharpened in timing: provisional § 1519 relief is live, which means collection is stayed, but the recognition order — the mechanism that makes that stay durable — has not yet issued. 
Under the terms presented to the Israeli court, Papaya will transfer available cash balances into a designated fund overseen by a court-appointed official, with that fund expected to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 as a potential source for settling claims should the U.S. ruling become enforceable in Israel.
 
The $719 million disgorgement figure was entered in lieu of the $420 million in actual damages awarded by the jury in April 2026, as Firy is entitled to recover once for its injury.
 The gap between the fund's projected 2026 ceiling and the judgment face value is the central recovery constraint, and the pace at which that fund is populated — and by whom it is overseen — will deserve close attention as the Israeli proceeding develops in parallel. The next concrete milestone in Delaware is the recognition hearing scheduled by Dkt. 40; that date governs when Judge Walrath can enter the order that would make the automatic-stay effect of § 1520 operative against Firy's collection efforts on a permanent rather than provisional basis.
